analysis.one_liner: Conditions federal airport grants on paying airport service workers at least $15 an hour with benefits.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a House vote: it sat in the Transportation and Infrastructure Committee from June 2022 until the Congress ended in January 2023, despite 90 cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have required large, medium, and small hub airports to certify that their service workers — baggage handlers, wheelchair agents, security officers, cleaners, food and retail staff — are paid at least the higher of $15 an hour, the federal service-contract prevailing wage, or the local minimum wage, plus minimum fringe benefits [S2] [S3]. Airports that did not comply would lose access to federal airport development grants, including money from the 2021 infrastructure law [S3]. It was introduced in June 2022, referred to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee, and never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the Congress ended [S1] [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Airport service workers — security officers, food service and retail staff, cleaners, ticketing and check-in agents, baggage and ramp handlers, and airline catering workers — at hub airports, who would be guaranteed the highest of $15 an hour, the local prevailing wage under the Service Contract Act, or the state or local minimum wage, plus minimum fringe benefits, regardless of which contractor technically employs them [S2] [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Sets a wage and benefits floor covering security officers, food service workers, cleaning staff, ticketing agents, retail workers, baggage handlers, wheelchair assistants, and airline catering workers at every small, medium, and large hub airport [S2] [S3].

The floor is the highest of $15 per hour, the Labor Department's Service Contract Act prevailing wage and benefits for the locality and job class, the federal contractor minimum wage, or the applicable state or local minimum wage — so it lifts pay most where local standards are weakest [S3].

The requirement follows the worker, not the employer: it applies regardless of any contracting arrangement between the worker, contractor, or subcontractor, closing the common loophole where airlines shift low-wage work to subcontractors [S3].

Enforcement is tied to money airports already depend on: the Transportation Secretary may approve airport development grants, passenger facility charge uses, and discretionary grants only for compliant airports, and 2021 infrastructure law airport grants and terminal funds are restricted to compliant sponsors [S3].
It does not override stronger state or local wage laws, so cities with higher minimums keep their higher standards [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Airport owners and operators and the contractors that staff concessions, cleaning, security, and ground handling, who would bear the higher wage and benefits costs to keep receiving federal airport grants; some of that cost could reach travelers through higher concession prices, and airports that refused to comply would forfeit federal development funding [S3].

drawbacks.text: The bill's enforcement runs on paperwork: airport sponsors certify compliance annually and collect certifications from employers, but the bill text specifies no audits, penalties, or private right of action for workers who are underpaid, so a noncompliant contractor's exposure is mainly losing the airport its grant eligibility [S3].

Higher mandated wages and benefits for contractors raise operating costs at hub airports; some of that could be passed to travelers through higher food, retail, and service prices, and airports that chose not to comply would lose access to federal development grants, potentially delaying projects [S3].

Tying infrastructure money to a labor standard adds a condition to federal airport grants that opponents of such conditions generally argue limits local airport flexibility over how to spend the funds [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is a hard wage and benefits floor for some of the lowest-paid workers in aviation, financed through a condition on federal grants the airports already receive, which is a relatively low-cost lever for the public. The design weaknesses are real: compliance rests on annual self-certification with no specified audits or penalties, and the practical remedy for a violating airport is losing grant money — a blunt instrument that could hurt travelers if an airport chose noncompliance over a project. On balance the bill's benefits to workers would likely outweigh those costs, but its enforcement would depend heavily on how seriously the Transportation Secretary policed the certifications.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee in June 2022, passed along to its Aviation Subcommittee the next day, and never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

narrative.text: Rep. Chuy Garcia introduced the bill on June 16, 2022, and 90 House members — all Democrats — signed on as cosponsors [S1] [S4] [S5].
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure, and on June 17 it was referred to that committee's Subcommittee on Aviation [S5].
No further action appears in the record: the bill never received a markup, a committee vote, or a floor vote, and it died when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Hub airports and the contractors that employ airport service workers are better off, because they avoided the wage and benefits requirement while keeping unrestricted access to federal airport grants, including infrastructure-law funds.

sides.party_line_note: All 90 cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican signed on; the bill then died in committee without ever reaching a floor vote, so the only recorded position is the partisan split in sponsorship.

industries.industry: Airport service contractors (janitorial, security, food service, retail, and ground-handling companies)
industries.note: They employ most covered workers and would have had to pay at least $15 an hour or the prevailing wage plus benefits; their labor costs would rise at every hub airport. The bill died before taking effect, so their costs stayed where they were.

They would have had to certify worker pay annually and risk losing Airport Improvement Program, terminal, and infrastructure-law grant funds if they or their contractors failed to comply — a compliance burden and a condition on money they currently receive unconditionally.

Airlines largely do not directly employ these workers, but many contract out baggage handling, cleaning, and catering, so higher contractor wages could feed into airline service costs; the bill excludes mechanical and maintenance functions from coverage.

A higher wage and benefits floor across hub airports raises the baseline the bill's union allies organize around, and the bill explicitly applies to workers under collective bargaining agreements rather than exempting them.
